caption:
A sharper image of an old picture is still an old picture. Resolution tells you how clearly you can see a feature. It says nothing about when that feature was last observed.

A site imaged once a month at high resolution can miss a structure built and torched inside that gap. A site imaged every few days at lower resolution catches the sequence — bare ground, construction, activity, removal — even if no single frame is crisp. For most security and infrastructure questions, the sequence matters more than the snapshot.

This is why a collection plan should be built around revisit cadence first, resolution second. Ask what changes over what interval before asking how sharp the picture needs to be. Get the cadence wrong and no amount of detail recovers the gap.
thread: Resolution tells you how clear the picture is. Revisit cadence tells you whether you had a picture when it mattered. Most people optimize the wrong one first.
A monthly high-res pass can miss a structure built and burned inside the gap. A frequent lower-res pass catches the sequence: bare ground, build, activity, removal.
For pattern-of-life and change detection, sequence beats sharpness. A blurry timeline still tells you something happened. A single sharp frame taken at the wrong moment tells you nothing.
Build the collection plan around the question first: what changes, over what interval. Set cadence to match that interval. Then pick the resolution you can afford.
Get cadence wrong and no amount of detail fixes it after the fact.

card.headline: Frequency beats sharpness
card.sub: A clear image taken at the wrong moment tells you nothing. Revisit cadence decides what you see. Resolution only decides how well.

rationale: Fills a genuinely untouched explainer gap (cadence vs. resolution) with a concrete, teachable mental model and no product pitch.
